names.name: Sawdah
names.morphology: Classical Arabic substantive noun (pattern faʿlah) from the root s-w-d, signifying preeminence, sovereignty, nobility of lineage, and fertile green land.
names.short_meaning: Noble sovereign, fertile expanse; Mother of the Believers Sawdah bint Zam'ah.
names.primary_meaning: Sawdah (سَوْدَة) is a historic Arabic feminine given name meaning 'noble sovereign', 'eminent in dignity', or 'fertile, lush landscape'. In Islamic history, it is the illustrious name of Mother of the Believers Sawdah bint Zam'ah al-Qurashiyyah, the first woman the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ married after the passing of Khadijah, celebrated for her profound generosity and early migration to Abyssinia.
names.literal_meaning: Derived from siyādah (mastery, nobility, and preeminent honor), or referring to fertile, dark-green soil teeming with life.
names.meaning_explanation: The root s-w-d denotes nobility, leadership (sayyid), and lush fertility. Sawdah bint Zam'ah was an early convert in Mecca who bravely migrated to Abyssinia with her first husband. After his death, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ married her in Mecca, bringing comfort and maternal care to his household. She was renowned for her cheerful good nature, towering devotion, and extraordinary charity, frequently giving away large gifts of wealth the moment she received them.
names.semantic_domain: Nobility, Mother of the Believers, generosity, companion name

quranic.note: The personal name Sawdah is not in the Qur'an; she is honored in the collective address to the Mothers of the Believers in Surah al-Ahzab (33:32).

hadith_status.note: Prominently featured in Sahih al-Bukhari (5206) and Sahih Muslim (1463) detailing her marriage, selflessness, and the high praise bestowed on her by Aisha.

prophetic_status.note: Not the name of a prophet; belongs to the Mother of the Believers and wife of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.

companion_status.note: Sawdah bint Zam'ah al-Amiriyyah al-Qurashiyyah (d. 54 AH / 674 CE), Mother of the Believers, buried in al-Baqi' in Medina.

names.religion_association: Wife of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ; revered Mother of the Believers (Umm al-Mu'minin)
names.religious_status: Name of an eminent Mother of the Believers held in the utmost reverence and love by all Muslims worldwide.
names.religious_explanation: Named after Sawdah bint Zam'ah, whose selflessness and loyalty to the Prophet ﷺ was so pure that Aisha famously said: 'No woman was more beloved to me that I should be in her shoes than Sawdah bint Zam'ah.'
names.cultural_note: A deeply respected traditional name across the Muslim world representing devotion, dignity, maternal warmth, and supreme charity.
names.cultural_interpretation: Chosen to inspire unselfish generosity, steadfast loyalty in adversity, high moral dignity, and love for the Prophet's household.
names.usage_note: Frequently chosen across Arab and Muslim families; consistently documented in civil registries and religious compendia.

names.name: Thumamah
names.morphology: Classical Arabic substantive noun from thumām (a resilient, flexible, and sweet desert grass), symbolizing adaptability, vitality, and resilience.
names.short_meaning: Resilient desert plant; companion Thumamah ibn Uthal, chieftain of Yamama.
names.primary_meaning: Thumamah (ثُمَامَة) is an Arabic masculine given name meaning 'a resilient desert plant' or 'pliant, sweet-natured vitality'. In Islamic history, it is the renowned name of Thumamah ibn Uthal al-Hanafi, chieftain of the Banu Hanifa, whose transformation upon witnessing the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in Medina led to one of the most famous conversions in early Islam.
names.literal_meaning: A stalk or bundle of thumām (a sweet-scented desert grass noted for bendable resilience in dry winds).
names.meaning_explanation: Thumamah was captured as a prisoner of war and tied to a pillar in the Prophet's Mosque in Medina. The Prophet ﷺ treated him with gracious hospitality for three days without coercion. When released unconditionally, Thumamah walked to a nearby palm grove, washed himself, and returned to declare Islam before the Prophet ﷺ. He then went directly to Mecca to perform Umrah, becoming the first Muslim to openly recite the Talbiyah before the Quraysh.
names.semantic_domain: Chieftaincy, conversion, Umrah, moral courage, companion name

quranic.note: Thumamah is not mentioned in the Qur'an; his dramatic conversion and fidelity are immortalized in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim.

hadith_status.note: Narrated in detail in Sahih al-Bukhari (4372) and Sahih Muslim (1764) recounting his capture, dignified treatment, and conversion.

prophetic_status.note: Not the name of a prophet; belongs to an illustrious Companion.

companion_status.note: Thumamah ibn Uthal al-Hanafi (d. 12 AH / 633 CE), chieftain of Yamama, hero of the Ridda wars, martyr for the faith.

names.religion_association: Premier example of sincere conversion through prophetic grace; first open pilgrim in Mecca
names.religious_status: Name of an esteemed Sahabi remembered for courageous loyalty to Islam and standing firm against apostasy in Yamama.
names.religious_explanation: Named after Thumamah ibn Uthal, whose story is universally studied as proof that Islamic conversion is built upon genuine conviction inspired by prophetic character.
names.cultural_note: A noble classical Arabic name celebrated in tribal and Islamic historiography for supreme moral dignity and courage.
names.cultural_interpretation: Chosen to inspire independent judgment, moral clarity, dignified leadership, and resolute defense of truth.
names.usage_note: A respected, classical name widely documented in early Islamic chronicles and modern Arab civil registers.

names.name: Buraydah
names.morphology: Classical Arabic diminutive noun (pattern fuʿaylah) from bard, meaning 'refreshing cool breeze', 'soothing drops of hail', or 'gentle relief'.
names.short_meaning: Cool refreshing breeze; companion Buraydah ibn al-Husayb al-Aslami.
names.primary_meaning: Buraydah (بُرَيْدَة) is an Arabic masculine given name meaning 'refreshing cool breeze', 'soothing relief', or 'delicate pearl of coolness'. In Islamic history, it is the renowned name of Buraydah ibn al-Husayb al-Aslami, the companion who met the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ during the Hijrah with seventy riders of his tribe, embraced Islam instantly, and raised his turban as a white banner of peace.
names.literal_meaning: Diminutive of bardah (coolness, pleasant breeze), symbolizing peace, tranquility, and the alleviation of burning desert heat.
names.meaning_explanation: During the Hijrah, Buraydah and seventy men rode out to capture the Prophet ﷺ. When the Prophet asked his name and he replied 'Buraydah' (coolness), the Prophet turned to Abu Bakr and said: 'Your matter has become cool and easy.' When he asked about his tribe and he said 'Aslam' (peace), the Prophet said: 'You are saved.' Buraydah and all seventy men accepted Islam on the spot.
names.semantic_domain: Peace, good omen, Hijrah, banner of faith, companion name

quranic.note: Buraydah is not in the Qur'an; his historical conversion during the Hijrah is chronicled in classical Sira and hadith collections.

hadith_status.note: Documented in Sahih al-Bukhari (3816) and Dalā'il al-Nubuwwah by al-Bayhaqi recounting the encounter during the Hijrah.

prophetic_status.note: Not the name of a prophet; belongs to an early revered Companion.

companion_status.note: Buraydah ibn al-Husayb al-Aslami (d. 62 AH / 682 CE), standard-bearer of the Hijrah, veteran of Khaybar, buried in Marw.

names.religion_association: Standard-bearer of the Hijrah; prolific transmitter of prophetic traditions
names.religious_status: Name of an esteemed Sahabi praised for immediate submission to truth and steadfast companionship across Khaybar and Tabuk.
names.religious_explanation: Named after Buraydah ibn al-Husayb, who transformed a hostile pursuit into an enduring pact of peace and brotherhood with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
names.cultural_note: A prestigious name in Arab history, also giving its name to the famous historical oasis city of Buraidah in al-Qassim, Saudi Arabia.
names.cultural_interpretation: Chosen to inspire peace, pleasant ease, sudden divine guidance, and dependable loyalty.
names.usage_note: Commonly documented across the Arabian Peninsula, especially in Saudi Arabia; recognized in classical biographical dictionaries.

names.name: Zunairah
names.morphology: Classical Arabic diminutive noun (pattern fuʿaylah) from zinnār, denoting a delicate adorned sash or belt of dignity, fine craftsmanship, and modest ornament.
names.short_meaning: Adorned sash of dignity; early heroine and martyr of faith Zunairah al-Rumiyyah.
names.primary_meaning: Zunairah (زُنَيْرَة) is an Arabic feminine given name meaning 'delicate sash of honor', 'adorned belt of dignity', or 'flower of steadfast faith'. In Islamic history, it is the renowned name of Zunairah al-Rumiyyah, an early convert to Islam who endured brutal torture in Mecca until she lost her sight, yet remained unshakeable in faith until Allah miraculously restored her vision.
names.literal_meaning: Diminutive of zinnār (a belt or sash of modest beauty), signifying strength, neat elegance, and steadfast commitment.
names.meaning_explanation: Zunairah was among the enslaved early converts in Mecca who had no tribal protector. Abu Jahl and other chieftains severely tortured her to force her to renounce Islam, causing her to lose her sight. When the polytheists mocked her claiming their idols took her sight, she proclaimed with supreme courage that idols neither see nor harm and that only Allah has power. The very next morning, Allah restored her eyesight completely. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq then purchased and freed her.
names.semantic_domain: Steadfast faith, miracle of healing, early Meccan sacrifice, Sahabiyyah name

quranic.note: Zunairah does not appear by name in the Qur'an; her heroic endurance is chronicled in the earliest works of prophetic Sira.

hadith_status.note: Documented in Ibn Hisham's Sirah and Al-Isabah (Entry 11226) as one of the seven oppressed early believers purchased and emancipated by Abu Bakr.

prophetic_status.note: Not a prophet's name; it is the name of an illustrious early female Companion (Sahabiyyah).

companion_status.note: Zunairah al-Rumiyyah (early 7th century CE), pioneer convert, symbol of spiritual triumph over persecution, freed by Abu Bakr.

names.religion_association: Early Meccan martyrs and heroes of faith; triumph of monotheism over idolatrous tyranny
names.religious_status: Name of an extraordinary Sahabiyyah celebrated across Islamic history as a living miracle of divine healing and resolute conviction.
names.religious_explanation: Named after Zunairah, whose refusal to bow before oppression and subsequent divine healing remains a timeless monument of steadfastness (Sabr) in Islam.
names.cultural_note: A deeply beloved, poetic name widely cherished across South Asia, the Middle East, and Western Muslim communities.
names.cultural_interpretation: Chosen to inspire unyielding moral courage, inner light, spiritual resilience, and total trust in Allah's mercy.
names.usage_note: A highly popular and celebrated feminine name in contemporary Muslim societies, backed by authentic classical historical documentation.

names.name: Murarah
names.morphology: Classical Arabic substantive noun (pattern fuʿālah) signifying endurance, intense persistence, and firmness of resolution.
names.short_meaning: Enduring firmness; Badri companion Murarah ibn al-Rabi' al-Amiri.
names.primary_meaning: Murarah (مُرَارَة) is a historic Arabic masculine name meaning 'enduring firmness', 'unbending resolution', or 'perseverance'. In Islamic history, it is the renowned name of Murarah ibn al-Rabi' al-Amiri al-Ansari, a veteran of Badr and one of the three truthful companions whose repentance and honesty were immortalized and forgiven by Allah in the Holy Qur'an.
names.literal_meaning: Derived from marrah (strength, firmness, and endurance), signifying unyielding moral resolve and steadfast character.
names.meaning_explanation: Murarah ibn al-Rabi' fought bravely at Badr and Uhud. When the expedition to Tabuk occurred, he lagged behind without hypocrisy, simply overtaken by hesitation. When the Prophet ﷺ returned, Murarah refused to make False excuses, choosing complete honesty. After fifty days of social boycott and heartfelt repentance, Allah sent down divine forgiveness in Surah at-Tawbah (9:118).
names.semantic_domain: Truthfulness, repentance, Badr, Quranic forgiveness, companion name

quranic.note: Direct subject of divine forgiveness revealed in Surah at-Tawbah (9:118): 'وَعَلَى الثَّلَاثَةِ الَّذِينَ خُلِّفُوا' (And to the three who were left behind).

hadith_status.note: Documented in Sahih al-Bukhari (4418) and Sahih Muslim (2769) in the famous hadith of Ka'b ibn Malik naming Murarah as one of the upright veterans of Badr.

prophetic_status.note: Not the name of a prophet; belongs to a distinguished Ansari Badri Companion.

companion_status.note: Murarah ibn al-Rabi' al-Amiri al-Ansari (d. 25 AH / 646 CE), veteran of Badr, subject of Qur'an 9:118.

names.religion_association: Subject of divine Quranic revelation; exemplar of honesty and sincere repentance (Tawbah)
names.religious_status: Name of an esteemed Sahabi chosen by the Prophet ﷺ as an exemplar of the noble veterans of Badr who never lied.
names.religious_explanation: Named after Murarah ibn al-Rabi', whose refusal to deceive the Prophet ﷺ earned him eternal divine praise and acceptance in the text of the Holy Qur'an.
names.cultural_note: A prestigious historical name held in great esteem in Islamic theology and ethics as proof of the power of sincere truthfulness.
names.cultural_interpretation: Chosen to inspire absolute truthfulness in speech, courage to admit error, heartfelt repentance, and steadfast endurance.
names.usage_note: A classical Arabic name documented in the foundational records of Quranic commentary and hadith.

names.name: Kharijah
names.morphology: Classical Arabic active participle form (pattern fāʿilah) from kharaja, denoting one who emerges prominent, distinguished, and preeminent above the crowd.
names.short_meaning: Prominent, distinguished leader; Badri companion Kharijah ibn Zayd al-Ansari.
names.primary_meaning: Kharijah (خَارِجَة) is a historic Arabic masculine given name meaning 'prominent leader', 'one who emerges distinguished', or 'preeminent champion'. In Islamic history, it is the renowned name of Kharijah ibn Zayd al-Ansari, chieftain of the Khazraj who pledged allegiance at the Second Pledge of Aqaba, fought at Badr, and was paired by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ as the brother of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq.
names.literal_meaning: Active participle signifying one who stands out prominently in excellence, valor, and conspicuous virtue.
names.meaning_explanation: The root kh-r-j signifies emerging into the open, excelling, and prominence. Kharijah ibn Zayd was one of the Medinan chieftains who welcomed the Prophet ﷺ. When the Prophet established the brotherhood (Mu'akhah) between the Emigrants and Helpers, he paired his closest companion, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, with Kharijah. At the Battle of Uhud, Kharijah fought with extraordinary bravery until he attained martyrdom, receiving over ten mortal wounds defending the Prophet.
names.semantic_domain: Bravery, brotherhood, Badr, Uhud martyr, companion name

quranic.note: Kharijah is not mentioned in the Qur'an; his historical honor is established in authentic hadith and Sahaba chronicles.

hadith_status.note: Documented in Sahih al-Bukhari (3929) and Sunan an-Nasa'i detailing his martyrdom at Uhud and burial in a shared grave with Sad ibn al-Rabi'.

companion_status.note: Kharijah ibn Zayd al-Ansari (martyred 3 AH / 625 CE at Uhud), brother of Abu Bakr in Islam and hero of Badr.

names.name: Mijzaz
names.morphology: Classical Arabic intensive instrument/agent noun (pattern mifʿāl) from jazza, denoting an incisive, penetrating observer who discerns fine distinctions with clarity.
names.short_meaning: Incisive observer; companion Mijzaz al-Mudliji, famed physiognomist.
names.primary_meaning: Mijzaz (مِجْزَاز) is an authentic Arabic masculine given name meaning 'incisive, sharp-sighted observer' or 'one of keen discernment'. In Islamic history, it is the renowned name of Mijzaz al-Mudliji, the famed companion and master of physiognomy (Qiyāfah) whose accurate observation of the lineage of Usama ibn Zayd brought joy and radiant delight to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.
names.literal_meaning: Derived from jazza (to cut cleanly, sever doubt, or decide decisively), signifying a sharp mind and decisive insight.
names.meaning_explanation: During pre-Islamic times, hypocrites cast slurs against Usama ibn Zayd because he was dark-skinned while his father Zayd was fair. One day, Zayd and Usama were sleeping under a cloak with only their feet exposed. Mijzaz passed by and remarked: 'These feet are from one another.' In Sahih al-Bukhari, Aisha narrates that the Prophet ﷺ entered her room with his blessed face shining like a mirror with joy because Mijzaz's expert confirmation silenced the slanderers.
names.semantic_domain: Discernment, wisdom, prophetic joy, companion name

quranic.note: Mijzaz is not in the Qur'an; his historical contribution in confirming truth and bringing joy to the Prophet ﷺ is recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim.

hadith_status.note: Recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari (3555, 6770) and Sahih Muslim (1459) where the Prophet ﷺ rejoices at Mijzaz's testimony.

prophetic_status.note: Not the name of a prophet; belongs to an early revered Companion.

names.name: Bujayr
names.morphology: Classical Arabic diminutive noun (pattern fuʿayl) of abjar, signifying broadhearted generosity, cheerful vitality, and abundant ease.
names.short_meaning: Generous and cheerful; companion Bujayr ibn Zuhayr.
names.primary_meaning: Bujayr (بُجَيْر) is an authentic Arabic masculine given name meaning 'broadhearted', 'generous in spirit', or 'prosperous and cheerful'. In Islamic history, it is the renowned name of Bujayr ibn Zuhayr al-Muzani, an early convert who fought at Hunayn and Ta'if, whose poetic letter to his brother Ka'b ibn Zuhayr led to Ka'b's famous conversion and the recitation of the prophetic praise poem Banat Su'ad.
names.literal_meaning: Diminutive form of abjar, expressing affectionate broadness of chest, magnanimity, and rich hospitality.
names.meaning_explanation: Bujayr was the son of the great pre-Islamic poet Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma. He traveled to Medina and embraced Islam enthusiastically. When his brother Ka'b composed verses mocking his conversion, Bujayr wrote back urging him with heartfelt brotherly wisdom to abandon False gods and seek the forgiveness of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. His letter transformed Ka'b's heart, leading to his journey to Medina and the presentation of the Prophet's mantle (Burdah).

quranic.note: Bujayr is not mentioned in the Qur'an; his historical role in early Islamic literary history is recorded in authentic Sira.

names.short_meaning: Dignified guiding staff; companion Mihjan ibn al-Adra' al-Aslami.
names.primary_meaning: Mihjan (مِحْجَن) is an Arabic masculine given name meaning 'guiding staff of dignity', 'support in the path of truth', or 'steadfast guide'. In Islamic history, it is the renowned name of Mihjan ibn al-Adra' al-Aslami, an early convert who built the mosque of Banu Aslam and transmitted important hadiths regarding congregational prayer and the virtues of Medina.
names.literal_meaning: A curved staff or cane used for walking with dignity and guiding mounts, symbolizing steady support and leadership.
names.meaning_explanation: Mihjan ibn al-Adra' was a devoted companion who accompanied the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in Medina. The Prophet loved to visit his tribal mosque. In Sahih Muslim and Sunan an-Nasa'i, Mihjan narrates that the Prophet ﷺ took him by the hand to look out over Medina from a mountain path, declaring its sacred inviolability and praising the tranquility of its believers.

names.name: Salsal
names.morphology: Qur'anic Arabic substantive noun from the reduplicated root ṣ-l-ṣ-l, designating pure, dry, resounding clay from which human creation was divinely fashioned.
names.short_meaning: Pure resounding clay; directly attested Qur'anic term.
names.primary_meaning: Salsal (صَلْصَال) is a Qur'anic masculine given name meaning 'pure resounding clay' or 'the wondrous substance of creation'. It is directly attested in the Holy Qur'an in Surah al-Rahman (55:14) and Surah al-Hijr (15:26, 28, 33) describing the primordial material from which Allah created humanity before breathing into it the spirit of life.
names.literal_meaning: Dry, pure clay that produces a clear, resonant sound when touched, signifying cohesive strength, purity, and the marvel of divine craftsmanship.
names.meaning_explanation: In Surah al-Rahman (55:14), Allah declares: 'خَلَقَ الْإِنسَانَ مِن صَلْصَالٍ كَالْفَخَّارِ' ('He created man from clay like that of pottery'). Classical commentators such as Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari explain that salsal represents pure clay that has dried until it resounds, illustrating the profound Quranic truth that humble earthly dust is elevated through divine will into conscious, noble beings.
names.semantic_domain: Creation, divine craftsmanship, humility, Quranic term

quranic.note: Directly attested in the Qur'an in Surah al-Rahman (55:14) and Surah al-Hijr (15:26, 28, 33).

prophetic_status.note: Not a prophet's name; it is a scriptural Qur'anic noun designating the origin of human creation.

names.religious_status: Direct Qur'anic vocabulary with deep philosophical and spiritual resonance reminding humanity of its origin and dignity.
names.religious_explanation: Named after the Quranic primordial clay, symbolizing genuine humility before God, cohesive strength, and wonder at divine creation.
names.cultural_note: A resonant, distinctive Qur'anic name favored by families seeking a name rooted in the majestic verses of Surah al-Rahman.
names.cultural_interpretation: Chosen to evoke humility, groundedness, moral strength, and constant remembrance of our origin and return to Allah.
